title: Jobs: the step vocabulary, execution, checkpoint and resume
summary: A job is an ordered list of steps drawn from a closed ten-kind vocabulary the database owns (farm.step_kinds), run against one leased device by internal/runner. Only three things end a step badly: its own timeout, an error nothing can retry, or the job's max_runtime. A dropped ADB socket is none of those — it is retried inside the lease with no attempt cap, bounded only by a deadline the job's author wrote down. Long work belongs in a shell_detached step, because that is the only kind whose result lives on the device instead of in a socket the control plane happens to be holding.

sections.heading: What a job may do to a lease, and what it may not
sections.source: internal/runner/runner.go:1-53 (package doc), 160-176 (Holder), internal/runner/steps.go:28-56 (Conn), internal/jobrunner/jobrunner.go:1-72 (package doc), internal/jobrunner/conn.go:1-105
sections.body:
The runner is handed a `Holder` interface two methods wide — `Context()` and `Fenced()`. There is no `Release`, no `Renew`, no `Witness`. That is enforcement, not convention: **a socket error inside a step has nowhere to travel except back to its caller as a Go error**, because nothing in the runner's reach can end a lease.

The same discipline runs down through `runner.Conn` (three methods — Shell, Push, Pull; no health, no reconnect, no lease handle) and into `jobrunner.DeviceConn`, which is a translation with no retry and no timeout of its own. A five-second timeout invented in the adapter would silently overrule a thirty-minute budget a job's author wrote down.

The jobrunner states the boundary from the other side: "farm.leases.release_reason has no connectivity value, so there is no word for it to write."

Exactly four endings exist, and they are the vocabulary of `farm.job_attempts.outcome`:

The one that matters at 3am is **abandoned**. It means the attempt stopped without a verdict — SIGTERM, node drain, pod eviction, or the lease being fenced. The job row is not touched, the lease is deliberately **not** released, and `farm.jobs.checkpoint` stays where it is. The replacement process re-acquires the same lease by job id (`farm.lease_acquire` is idempotent on job_id and does **not** bump the fence), gets the same device at the **same fence**, and resumes. Releasing on shutdown would hand a half-finished six-hour job's device to somebody else.

Fencing is not a connectivity event. `lease.ErrFenced` is returned only when `farm.lease_renew` matches zero rows (internal/lease/store.go:77-80) — the database saying somebody else holds this lease. A dial failure or a timeout against Postgres is explicitly not fencing.
bullets: A step that has been retrying a dead socket for twenty minutes still holds its device. The only thing that will take it away is the step's own timeout, `max_runtime`, or a human.
`aborted` in `farm.job_steps.state` means the run context ended mid-step — fenced or shutting down. It is not the step failing; it was stopped.
The one exception: when the run context ends because `max_runtime` elapsed, the step is recorded `failed`, not `aborted`, because that clock is the user's own (runner.go:619-622).

rows: a step ended badly, or max_runtime elapsed, or the spec cannot parse
`failed`, or back to `queued` if attempts remain and the failure is not permanent
a human ended it before this placement ran
fenced, or the process is shutting down
untouched — the checkpoint is the handover

sections.heading: The vocabulary is closed, and the database owns it
sections.source: migrations/00004_operate.sql:154-174, internal/jobspec/spec.go:1-66 and 84-116, internal/jobspec/spec_test.go:27-60, internal/api/specs.go:120-145 and 618-700, internal/runner/runner.go:893-906
sections.body:
`farm.jobs.spec` is a `jsonb` column and anything fits in one. That is exactly why the step vocabulary is not defined in Go: it is the rows of `farm.step_kinds`, and `farm.job_steps.kind` is a foreign key against it. `internal/jobspec` restates those rows, and `TestKindTableMatchesMigration` reads `migrations/00004_operate.sql` and fails if the two ever drift.

The runner asks the database again at run time (`loadKinds`, runner.go:1017), so a binary whose migrations are behind refuses a job rather than half-executing it.

Two booleans per row are behaviour, not documentation:

- **idempotent** decides whether a resume may re-run an interrupted step. `false` means a crash mid-step is not recoverable by repeating it.
- **needs_artifact** decides whether the payload must name content by sha256. Validation requires 64 lowercase hex characters, mirroring `CHECK (sha256 ~ '^[0-9a-f]{64}$')` on `farm.artifacts`.

A kind this binary does not know is **refused at parse time, never skipped** — a skipped step is a job that did less than it says it did. `GET /api/v1/specs/kinds` reports `supported:false` for a row the binary has no payload type for, and `disagrees_with_build:true` for a row whose flags differ from the compiled table, because that difference decides whether a resume may repeat a step.

Bounds, from the same endpoint's `limits` block: `max_steps` 1000, `max_step_id_len` 128, `max_artifact_name_len` 128, `max_step_timeout_s` 21600 (6h), `max_total_timeout_s` 86400 (24h), `max_expect_exit` 256. These are guards against a spec that could never succeed, not policy — the deadline anyone actually cares about is `farm.jobs.max_runtime`.

sections.heading: The shape of a step, and why a kind cannot lie about its payload
sections.body:
`Step` has no `Kind` field in Go. It has a payload, and the kind is derived from it (`Step.Kind`, spec.go:518). A struct with both admits `Kind: "push"` carrying an `Install` payload, and then every consumer has to decide which of the two to believe.

The wire form still carries an explicit `"kind"` key — jsonb is read by psql and by humans — and the payload lives under a key **named for its kind** (`"push": {...}`), not under a generic `"with"`. That buys two things: the jsonb is queryable by kind from SQL (`spec->'steps' @> '[{"install":{"sha256":"…"}}]'` finds every job that installed a given build), and a disagreement between the key and the payload is a shape error rather than a silent reinterpretation.

Decoding is strict in both directions. An unknown key is an error, not a dropped field, because a dropped field is a spec that means something other than what its author wrote — and because a spec written by a **newer** control plane must be refused by an older runner, not partially executed.

Every duration is a quoted Go duration string (`"90s"`, `"5m"`, `"2h30m"`), never a bare number. A number would have to mean seconds, or milliseconds, or nanoseconds, and whichever was chosen someone would eventually assume one of the other two — in a field that decides how long a phone is held.

Order is the only control flow. No branches, no loops, no conditionals, because a spec has to be resumable from a checkpoint in a different process on a different day, and "where was I" must be answerable with an index and a step id.

`jobspec.Parse` unmarshals **and** validates (spec.go:749). Anything that reaches the runner unvalidated is refused there, permanently — with a device already leased. See Gaps.
bullets: `id` — unique in the spec, `^[A-Za-z0-9][A-Za-z0-9._:/-]*$`, ≤128 chars. **Stable across edits**: `farm.jobs.checkpoint` and `farm.job_steps.step_id` both point at it.
`timeout` — bounds the step, retries included. Zero inherits `default_timeout`; the effective value must be positive or the spec is rejected.
`continue_on_error` — lets the job proceed when **this step** fails. It is about a non-zero exit or a failed assert, never about the transport, which never surfaces as a step failure at all.

Device paths are validated against `^(/[A-Za-z0-9._-]+)+$` with no `..` segment. A path that would need quoting is refused rather than quoted — these strings are interpolated into commands that run on a leased device.

All ten came back `valid:true, problem_count:0`. The two artifact-bearing kinds use `check_artifacts:false` because the digests they name are not in this farm's store; with the check on, the same specs report the digest absent (see the validation section).

Validation also enforces one artifact → one destination across the whole spec.

The APK is staged at `<work_dir>/<sha256>.apk`; nothing removes it afterwards, and `farm.device_artifacts` now records that this device holds those bytes — which is what lets the next job skip the transfer. `pm install` is checked twice, on exit status **and** on the presence of `Failure` in the output (steps.go:861), because older Android builds exit 0 while printing `Failure [INSTALL_FAILED_…]`.

examples.label: uninstall — "this package is absent afterwards"
examples.code:
{ "id": "clean/harness", "kind": "uninstall", "timeout": "5m",
  "uninstall": { "package": "com.acme.harness" } }
examples.output: uninstall       valid=True problems=0 steps=1 total_timeout_s=300
examples.note: Removing a package that is not installed is a **success**, and `farm.step_kinds` calls the kind idempotent on exactly that reading: the executor matches `not installed` / `unknown package` in the output and records `already_absent:true` (steps.go:889-896).

examples.label: shell — for commands that finish promptly
examples.code:
{ "id": "probe/sdk", "kind": "shell", "timeout": "1m",
  "shell": { "command": "getprop ro.build.version.sdk", "expect_exit": [0] } }
examples.output: shell           valid=True problems=0 steps=1 total_timeout_s=60
examples.note: `expect_exit` empty falls back to the spec's `default_expect_exit`, then to `{0}`. A shell stream that ends without an exit status is a **transport** error, not exit 0 — steps.go:263 refuses to read the zero-valued ExitCode as success.

examples.label: shell_detached — the device owns the result
examples.output: shell_detached  valid=True problems=0 steps=1 total_timeout_s=120
examples.note: `result_path` and `handle` must each be unique within the spec: two detached steps sharing one result file is one of them silently losing.

examples.label: wait_for — a deadline on the CONDITION, not on the connection
examples.output: wait_for        valid=True problems=0 steps=1 total_timeout_s=21600
examples.note: The step's own timeout must outlast the condition's, or the step would cut short a probe that was still allowed to succeed. Validation rejects `interval > timeout` (the probe would run once at most) and `wait_for.timeout > step timeout`.

examples.label: pull — names content that does not exist yet
examples.output: pull            valid=True problems=0 steps=1 total_timeout_s=600
examples.note: Unlike push and install, the digest is not known until the last byte has been read, so the bytes stream from the device straight into the content-addressed store through an `io.Pipe` (steps.go:921-935) — a two-gigabyte screen recording is a pipe, not an allocation. The resulting sha256 lands in `farm.job_steps.detail`. `artifact` is a name, not a path: no `/`.

examples.label: assert — a statement about the DEVICE's answer
examples.code:
{ "id": "check/sdk", "kind": "assert", "timeout": "1m",
  "assert": { "probe": "getprop ro.build.version.sdk", "op": "ge", "value": "29" } }
examples.output: assert          valid=True problems=0 steps=1 total_timeout_s=60
examples.note: Nine operators: `eq ne contains not_contains matches` (RE2 — no backreferences, no lookaround; compiled at validation and again at run time) and the numeric four `gt ge lt le`. A numeric operator with a non-numeric `value` is a validation error; a numeric operator whose **probe output** is not a number is a failed assertion, not an error (steps.go:1021-1026) — "your comparison is broken" and "the device said the wrong thing" call for different reactions.

examples.label: reset — a tier, expanded at run time from the profile
examples.code:
{ "id": "prep/reset", "kind": "reset", "timeout": "20m",
  "reset": { "tier": "medium" } }
examples.output: reset           valid=True problems=0 steps=1 total_timeout_s=1200 reset_steps=1
examples.note: `tier` must be spelled out: `ResetTier.Valid()` rejects the empty string, so the fallback in `execReset` to `farm.jobs.reset_tier` is unreachable through any validated spec. On this deployment the tier also does nothing at all — see Gaps.

examples.label: sleep — waited on the CONTROL PLANE, not on the device
examples.code:
{ "id": "soak/settle", "kind": "sleep", "timeout": "1m",
  "sleep": { "duration": "30s" } }
examples.output: sleep           valid=True problems=0 steps=1 total_timeout_s=60
examples.note: A `sleep` longer than the step that contains it can never finish, and validation says so. It is `time.After` in the runner process — it does not survive a process death, but it is idempotent, so a resume simply sleeps again.

sections.heading: A complete, validated spec using all ten kinds
sections.body:
Twelve steps, every kind, one reset expanded against the `default` profile.

Note `continue_on_error` on `collect/logcat`: a `logcat -d` that fails must not lose you the pull that follows it.

  "version": 1,
  "default_timeout": "5m",
  "default_expect_exit": [0],
  "steps": [
    { "id": "prep/reset", "kind": "reset", "timeout": "20m",
      "reset": { "tier": "medium" } },

    { "id": "prep/wait-boot", "kind": "wait_for", "timeout": "11m",
      "wait_for": { "probe": "[ \"$(getprop sys.boot_completed)\" = \"1\" ]",

      "push": { "sha256": "1111111111111111111111111111111111111111111111111111111111111111",
                "dest": "/data/local/tmp/farm/run_soak.sh", "mode": "0755" } },

      "install": { "sha256": "2222222222222222222222222222222222222222222222222222222222222222",
                   "reinstall": true, "grant": true } },

    { "id": "check/sdk", "kind": "assert",
      "assert": { "probe": "getprop ro.build.version.sdk", "op": "ge", "value": "29" } },

    { "id": "soak/start", "kind": "shell_detached", "timeout": "2m",
      "shell_detached": { "command": "sh /data/local/tmp/farm/run_soak.sh",
                          "result_path": "/data/local/tmp/farm/soak.result",
                          "handle": "soak" } },

    { "id": "soak/settle", "kind": "sleep", "timeout": "1m",
      "sleep": { "duration": "30s" } },

    { "id": "soak/await", "kind": "wait_for", "timeout": "6h",
      "wait_for": { "probe": "test -f /data/local/tmp/farm/soak.result",
                    "interval": "30s", "timeout": "5h59m" } },

    { "id": "soak/verdict", "kind": "shell",
      "shell": { "command": "cat /data/local/tmp/farm/soak.result", "expect_exit": [0] } },

    { "id": "collect/logcat", "kind": "shell", "timeout": "2m", "continue_on_error": true,
      "shell": { "command": "logcat -d > /data/local/tmp/farm/logcat.txt" } },

    { "id": "collect/pull-logcat", "kind": "pull", "timeout": "10m",
      "pull": { "path": "/data/local/tmp/farm/logcat.txt", "artifact": "logcat.txt" } },

    { "id": "cleanup/uninstall", "kind": "uninstall", "timeout": "5m",
      "uninstall": { "package": "com.acme.harness" } }

}

sections.heading: shell versus shell_detached, and why long work must be detached
sections.body:
A `shell` step keeps the ADB socket open until the command finishes. That makes the socket the source of truth for the result, and sockets to a rack of USB phones fail constantly. `shell_detached` removes the coupling: the command is daemonised, its output goes to a file on the **device**, and its exit status is published to `result_path` by an atomic rename. The ADB call returns as soon as the process is launched.

From that instant nothing about the run depends on a connection staying up. The host can lose the device for ten minutes; the pod can be evicted and replaced; the work carries on and the answer is still on the phone when the socket comes back. This is the direct countermeasure to DeviceFarmer/STF #663, where a ~90 minute ECONNRESET ended somebody's multi-hour run.

The wrapper the runner sends is:

```
mkdir -p <dir> || exit 1; rm -f <result> <tmp> <pid>; \
<prefix> sh -c 'echo $$ > <pid>; ( <command> ) > <log> 2>&1; echo $? > <tmp>; mv <tmp> <result>' \
  < /dev/null > /dev/null 2>&1 & echo started
```

Five details are load-bearing, and each is a specific way a six-hour run gets silently lost:

1. **The `mkdir` is fatal.** `result_path`'s directory comes from the spec and need not be somewhere the shell user can write. Everything after it is backgrounded with output discarded and the command ends in `echo started`, so without the guard a missing directory produces exit 0 for a command that never ran — and the job then sits in its `wait_for` until timeout, waiting for a result nothing will write.
2. **The command runs in a subshell `( … )`, not a brace group.** A brace group shares the wrapper's shell, so a harness script ending in `exit $rc` — which is how most of them end — would exit the wrapper too, before the status was recorded.
3. **The status is written to `<tmp>` and renamed.** A poll can never read a half-written status and conclude the command exited 0 when it exited 137.
4. **stdin and stdout are detached from the ADB stream.** Without that the shell service stays open until the command finishes, which is exactly the coupling this step exists to remove.
5. **The pid comes from `$$` inside the worker shell, not `$!` outside.** `setsid`'s own process exits immediately; its pid says nothing about whether the work is alive.

`detachPrefix` picks `nohup setsid` only when the prepare probe answered `setsid`; **any other answer, including an empty one, falls back to plain `nohup`**. The asymmetry is deliberate: guessing `setsid` onto a device that lacks it fails silently (the background launch still exits 0 while nothing runs), whereas guessing `nohup` onto a device that has `setsid` costs only the weaker guarantee.

**A detached command's exit code is not checked automatically.** Nothing in the runner reads the contents of `result_path` — `reattachDetached` only tests for the file's existence. To make a detached failure fail the job you need the triple: `shell_detached` → `wait_for` on the result file → a `shell` or `assert` that reads it.

sections.heading: A transport failure inside a step is retried, and never fails the job
sections.body:
When a device call fails, `Runner.retry` re-runs it with jittered exponential backoff — base 1s, cap 30s, doubling, then jittered uniformly over the top half of the window so an adb-server restart is not hit by every runner on the host in lockstep.

**There is no attempt cap.** The bound is the step's own timeout, a number the job's author wrote down. A hard-coded "three tries" would end a job because a USB hub took four seconds too long to come back.

The classification default is **retry**. An unclassified failure from a device connection is far more likely to be a cable, a hub or an adb server than a deliberate refusal, so only errors that positively cannot be fixed are marked `ErrNotRetryable`. Note what is *not* special-cased: `context.Canceled` and `context.DeadlineExceeded`. Every caller checks its own context first, so a context error reaching `isRetryable` came from a deadline **inside** the connection — a dial timeout, a read deadline — which is a transport failure wearing a context error's clothes.

`jobrunner.conn.classify` marks exactly three things non-retryable, and it is worth knowing which one you hit before you go looking at cables:

- **A non-transient `ProtocolError`** — a FAIL in the server's own words that will still be a FAIL next time. Deliberately absent from the transient list: `insufficient permissions`. A wrong udev rule stays wrong, and burning a step's budget to rediscover that sends an operator to look at cables instead of at the host.
- **`adbwire.ErrAmbiguousTarget`** — a devpath is a position in the USB tree and cannot be ambiguous, so this means the ADB server's view of the topology is broken. No number of retries fixes it.
- **`*adbwire.UsageError`** — caught before anything touched the wire: a malformed devpath, a request too large to frame. A caller bug.

Everything else is retried, including two cases that look like refusals:

- `adbwire.ErrNotFound` is a FAIL response but means "no transport at that position **right now**" — a USB re-enumeration, a phone rebooting.
- A FAIL whose reason contains `offline`, `unauthorized`, `still authorizing`, `still connecting`, `connecting to`, `protocol fault` or `closed`. Every reset tier above `none` reboots the phone, and those are the words the server speaks for the seconds afterwards. The match is against the FAIL's `Reason` field, not `err.Error()`, so a devpath containing one of these words cannot make a genuine refusal look transient.

`wait_for` is stricter still: a poll that fails on the wire is **counted and ignored**, not retried, because the condition it was asking about is unaffected. Only the condition's own timeout ends the wait unsatisfied.

The log line the retry loop emits is deliberately loud — `transport failure inside a step; retrying INSIDE the lease (job NOT failed)` — and its **absence from the lease log** is the proof the flapping cost the job nothing.

  FROM farm.job_steps WHERE detail ? 'transport_retries'

Read the three interesting rows: seven steps took five transport failures each and still reported **ok** — those are the runs #663 would have destroyed. The eight at six retries hit the step's own 30s timeout, which is the correct ending. The three at seven retries were still retrying when their lease was fenced, so they are `aborted`, not `failed` — the socket did not end them either.

sections.heading: What actually ends a job
sections.body:
Working through `execute`'s switch, in the order it applies:

1. **Run context aborted mid-step** → `classifyAbort` decides between three things that must never be collapsed: fenced (abandon, touch nothing), max_runtime (fail, **permanent**), or shutdown (abandon, lease left held).
2. **The step returned an error** — its own timeout, or something non-retryable. Step row `failed`. With `continue_on_error` it is marked `tolerated:true`, checkpointed done, and the job continues.
3. **The step ran and the device said no** (`Result.Failure`) — a non-zero exit outside `expect_exit`, a failed assert, a `pm install` that printed `Failure`. Same handling as (2).
4. Otherwise the step is `ok` and the checkpoint advances.

A failure at (2) or (3) is deliberately **not** marked permanent, even for a non-retryable error. The same failure on four different devices is what tells an operator this is a job problem, and `farm.job_attempts` is the table that shows it — declaring a verdict in the runner would replace that evidence with one process's opinion. So a failed attempt with budget left writes `farm.jobs.state = 'queued'`, not `'failed'`, and the scheduler places it elsewhere.

Only two things are permanent: a spec that cannot parse or validate (it will not parse next time either, and re-queueing would only burn devices), and an elapsed `max_runtime`.

Before the first step there is one more failure site: `prepare` creates the scratch directory and probes for setsid. It is retried like any other device call, bounded by the spec's own default step budget, and a device that stays unreachable for the whole of it fails the placement — **not permanently**, so the job goes back on the queue for a different phone.

`max_runtime` is computed by Postgres as `max_runtime - (now() - started_at)` and handed to the runner as a **duration**, never an instant (runner.go:983-988). No client clock is sent and none is compared. It is the one user-supplied clock in the whole system that may end a lease on its own.

Both terminal writes are fenced in SQL, not by hope. `writeJobState` requires the job to be non-terminal **and** a live lease (`state IN ('held','suspect')`) at this exact fence; zero rows updated means a newer holder owns it and this process's verdict is the stale one. That is logged, not raised.

sections.heading: Checkpoint: what it records and why
sections.body:
`farm.jobs.checkpoint` exists for one event, and it is the most ordinary event in a Kubernetes control plane: the pod running a job is evicted. Its replacement acquires the same lease by job id, gets the **same device at the same fence**, and must then answer a question the device cannot answer for it — which of these steps have already happened?

The checkpoint carries `version`, `attempt`, `fence`, `device_id`, `spec_hash`, `last_index`, `completed[]` and an optional `in_flight`. `updated_at` is added by Postgres inside the same statement; no client clock touches the row.

**The fence is what makes the record trustworthy.** It is monotonic and unique per lease, so a matching fence means no other holder has had the device in between — nobody has reset it, nothing has been reallocated, and the state the checkpoint describes is still on the hardware in front of us. A checkpoint from a different fence is not resumable, only re-runnable from the start.

`spec_hash` fingerprints the step list by **position, id and kind only**. Changing a timeout or a package name does not invalidate the record of which steps already ran; reordering or replacing them does.

The write is fenced in SQL: `WHERE COALESCE((checkpoint->>'fence')::bigint, 0) <= $3`. A process that lost its lease an hour ago and only now gets its statement through cannot clobber the progress of the attempt that replaced it. Zero rows is an ordinary, logged outcome — by then there is nothing left to abort and the server's checkpoint is newer anyway. A checkpoint that fails to land costs a re-run of one step, never the device, so it never ends a run.

A checkpoint that does not parse is treated as **absent**: the job starts over on a fresh placement, which is safe, rather than resuming against a structure this binary guessed at.

**When is the checkpoint written?** After every step that completes — and, critically, **before** any step whose kind is not idempotent. That ordering is the whole design: a crash between the `in_flight` write and the step's completion is recoverable as "we do not know" rather than inferred from silence.

examples.label: A checkpoint from a job run end to end
examples.code:
SELECT jsonb_pretty(checkpoint) FROM farm.jobs
 WHERE id = 'ac52f606-4115-43b3-a58c-c5eee949a0a3';
examples.note: Seven completed entries, elided above for width. There is no `in_flight` key: the last non-idempotent step finished, and `markDone` clears the marker. To browse checkpoints generally, use `WHERE checkpoint ? 'fence'` — filtering on `state='running'` returns nothing most of the time, because jobs on this farm finish in seconds.

examples.label: An in_flight marker: a non-idempotent step that was mid-run
examples.code:
SELECT id, state, checkpoint->'in_flight' AS in_flight
  FROM farm.jobs WHERE checkpoint ? 'in_flight' LIMIT 3;
examples.note: Six such rows exist. Each is a `shell` step (non-idempotent) written down before it ran, which then failed on its step timeout, so the marker was never cleared. Two of the three read `state = succeeded` while their own step row reads `failed` — that contradiction is the demo worker writing job state independently of the runner, not something production would produce (see Gaps). If one of these placements had been evicted rather than timing out, the resume would have **refused** — see the next section.

sections.heading: Resume: what is skipped, what is re-run, what is refused
sections.source: internal/runner/checkpoint.go:135-254 (plan, planResume), 256-259 (stepIsIdempotent), internal/runner/runner.go:407-425, 787-813 (reattach inside retry), internal/runner/steps.go:405-452 (reattachDetached)
sections.body:
`planResume` is the decision, taken before the first step runs, about what this attempt will skip, re-run or re-attach to. The rules in order:

1. **Not resuming** — a fresh placement, `farm.jobs.resumable = false`, or a checkpoint from another fence: everything runs. Fresh placements get a device that is not carrying our half-finished work.
2. **The spec must be the same list.** A mismatched `spec_hash`, a completed index past the end, or a completed id that no longer sits at its index → refuse. An operator editing a running job's spec is rare and legitimate; resuming index 4 of a list that no longer has the same steps at 0..3 is not.
3. **Steps in `completed` are skipped**, and get a `skipped` row with `reason: completed in an earlier attempt of this placement`.
4. **An in-flight step that is idempotent is simply re-run.** The authority is `farm.step_kinds.idempotent`, read from the database at run time — not remembered in Go — so a spec written today resumes tomorrow the way its author expected. An unrecognised kind defaults to **not** idempotent: a step nobody has classified must not be repeated on a guess.
5. **An in-flight `shell_detached` is re-attached to.** This is the case the whole design exists for. Its work is running *on the device*, so neither skipping it nor starting a second copy is correct.
6. **Anything else in flight is REFUSED**, and the refusal is marked permanent.

Rule 6 answers "why is a non-idempotent step not re-run". `shell` is marked non-idempotent precisely because re-running an interrupted one could repeat a side effect that may already have happened — an install, a payment, a factory reset. A job that fails with a clear message is strictly better than a farm that silently does things twice. It is permanent because re-queueing would run the whole spec again on a fresh device and repeat the very step we refused to repeat.

Note the asymmetry with retries: **inside** a step, a `shell` whose stream died without an exit status *is* retried, and can therefore run twice. That is safe because we still hold the device, we are certainly the only writer, and the command was started seconds ago. **Across** a process death none of that holds, so a resume refuses while a retry accepts. Work whose repetition would actually hurt belongs in `shell_detached`.

The re-attach probe sits **inside** the retry loop, not before it: "is this run already going on the device?" is exactly the question a flaky link must not be allowed to answer with "no". Its three legal answers are `done`, `running`, `absent`; **anything else is returned as an ordinary transport failure and asked again**, because the one reading it must never turn into is `absent`, which would start a second copy of a command that is running right now.

A resume does **not** spend an attempt. Re-attaching keeps the same attempt number, because burning budget on a pod eviction would spend a job's lives on the most ordinary event there is.

examples.label: The refusal message, verbatim from the source
examples.code:
runner: step %d (%s) of kind %s was interrupted and cannot be repeated safely
(farm.step_kinds says it is not idempotent); refusing to run it a second time —
a job whose long work runs in a shell_detached step resumes here instead, because
the device, not this process, owns that result
examples.note: internal/runner/checkpoint.go:240-248. The refused step gets its own `farm.job_steps` row with `detail: {"resume_refused": true}` (runner.go:541-546), so the reason survives in the table an operator reads. A refusal for a changed `spec_hash` carries no step index and therefore writes no such row — you will find that one only in the attempt's error text.

examples.label: The re-attach probe the runner sends
examples.code: if [ -f "<result_path>" ]; then echo done; elif [ -f "<dir>/<handle>.log" ]; then echo running; else echo absent; fi
examples.output: done | running | absent
examples.note: internal/runner/steps.go:411-414. `done` and `running` both mean "do not start a second copy" and produce a step row with `reattached: true` and `reattached_state`. Only `absent` — the previous process died between writing the checkpoint and launching anything — lets the step actually run. No resume has exercised this path on this deployment; the branch has no test either (see Gaps).

sections.heading: Attempts: telling a job problem from a device problem
sections.body:
`farm.job_attempts` is one row per time a job was placed on a device, keyed `UNIQUE (job_id, attempt)` and carrying `device_id`, `lease_id`, `fence`, `outcome` and `error`. Its purpose is stated in the migration: *a job that has been attempted on four devices and failed on all four is a job problem; the same failure on one device four times is a device problem.*

The attempt number is minted by a single `UPDATE farm.jobs SET attempt = attempt + 1 … RETURNING attempt`, so two schedulers racing the same job cannot mint the same number. The row goes down **before** the work does — and before any reason to refuse the work — because a placement that was refused is still a placement, and the table whose whole purpose is telling those two apart must see it.

`openAttempt` upserts: on conflict it resets `finished_at`, `outcome` and `error` to NULL. So a NULL outcome means "this attempt is open", which covers a running attempt, a resumed one, **and** an orphan whose process died. Only the age tells them apart.

Budget is `farm.jobs.max_attempts` (default 3, `CHECK >= 1`). Exceeding it is itself a failure with a named error. `jobrunner.finalize` mirrors the runner's re-queue decision, and when the runner's own write did not land it re-queues anyway: that guess is bounded by `max_attempts`, while a wrong `failed` is not recoverable at all.

How to read the table at 3am:
bullets: **N attempts, N distinct `device_id`, same `error`** → the job. Fix the spec.
**N attempts, one `device_id`, same `error`** → the device. Look at `farm.job_steps.detail->>'transport_retries'` for that attempt, then at the recovery ladder.
**`outcome = 'abandoned'`** → nothing failed. A pod died or a lease was fenced; the job kept its checkpoint. Three such rows exist on this farm, all from leases fenced mid-step.
**`outcome IS NULL` on a row older than a few minutes** → the process running it died without closing the row. Nothing sweeps these (see Gaps).

SELECT attempt, device_id, fence, outcome, left(coalesce(error,''),50) AS error,
       finished_at-started_at AS took
  FROM farm.job_attempts
 WHERE job_id = '0dc8994a-013c-43a7-b46b-2e35194cb86f' ORDER BY attempt;
examples.note: The full error on attempt 1 is `preparing the device work directory /data/local/tmp/device-farmer/0dc8994a-…: runner: step timeout elapsed` — the retries ran out the spec's own 30s budget, which is what ended it. The runner wrote `state='queued'` (not `failed`) because attempt 1 < max_attempts 3, the scheduler placed it on a different phone, and it finished in six seconds. Note there are **no** attempt-1 step rows: prepare failed before the first step. Six jobs on this farm reached `succeeded` on attempt 2 this way.

The socket did not end this — losing the lease did, and the runner wrote nothing further to the device and released nothing.

sections.heading: Reset tiers and their real expansions
sections.body:
`soft`, `medium` and `hard` mean nothing until somebody writes them down. Written down, from the profile's package list and nothing else:

- **none** — nothing at all.
- **soft** — clear the app data of every package the profile owns that is actually installed.
- **medium** — soft, then uninstall every third-party package **not** in the profile, then reapply `farm.device_state`.
- **hard** — medium, then reboot, wait out the shutdown, and wait for `boot_completed`.

The only input is the profile's package list, and that is what makes reset generic: the farm does not need to know what a job installed, because anything outside the profile is by definition not supposed to be there. It is also why medium's uninstall is *one* shell step that enumerates the device rather than a list of `uninstall` steps — the set is discovered on the device, at reset time, not guessed at when the spec was written.

Four details in the expansion are each a bug somebody already hit:

- **`reset/clear/<pkg>` tests for the package first.** `pm clear` prints `Failed` for a package that is not installed, and on a freshly enrolled phone none of the profile's packages are installed. Without the test, the very first reset of every new device fails, an attempt is charged, and a healthy phone is quarantined for being clean. `grep -qx` (not the exit code) decides the verdict, because `pm clear` exits 0 while printing `Failed` on several vendor builds, and `-x` anchors the whole line so a longer package name matched by `pm list packages`'s substring search cannot be mistaken for this one.
- **`reset/uninstall-unknown` runs `pm list packages -3` *before* the loop and checks it.** Inlined into a `for`, a package manager that is not answering yields an empty list, the loop runs zero times, and the step exits 0 — a reset reporting success having removed nothing, leaving one tenant's app installed for the next one.
- **`reset/reboot` carries `continue_on_error: true`.** The reboot severs the very socket that would report its exit code, so its self-report is worthless. This is not a transport failure being tolerated; it is a command whose success is only observable from the other side of it. `reset/boot-completed` is the actual proof.
- **`reset/reboot-settle` sleeps 30s (in a 45s step) and is not optional.** A device does not go down the instant `reboot` returns. Without the pause the probe reads `sys.boot_completed` from the system that is still shutting down, sees `1`, and declares the reset finished — and the job then starts on a device that reboots underneath it seconds later. Since `reset/reboot` cannot fail, this pause is the only thing that makes the probe's answer mean anything.

Three things happen in the executor rather than the expansion. The `device_state.sh` script is **written before the sub-steps run** (its content comes from `farm.device_state`, so it cannot be named by content hash in a spec, and a missing file makes the step fail loudly — which is right, because a missing script means durable state was *not* reapplied). The artifact ledger is **retracted before** a medium or hard wipe, not after: the dangerous direction is a `present` claim that outlives the content. And every sub-step runs against a copy of the environment carrying an **empty spec**, so a job that declared exit 1 a success for its own shell steps cannot thereby declare a failed `pm clear` a successful reset.

A transport failure during a reset re-runs the **whole** expansion, which is safe precisely because reset is idempotent — and it is why the expansion is a list of small steps rather than one long script. A sub-step's own deadline expiring is *not* laundered into transport noise; it becomes a non-retryable error naming the sub-step that hung (steps.go:1146-1153).

sections.heading: Validating before you file a job
sections.body:
`jobspec.Validate` returns **every** problem it finds, not the first, and each carries a JSON pointer in dotted form (`steps[3].push.dest`) so an editor can highlight the line. A person fixing a spec should need one round trip, not ten.

`POST /api/v1/specs/validate` accepts either the spec document itself as the body or `{"spec": …, "profile": …, "check_artifacts": …}` — an author pastes the file they are editing, a tool sends a request it composed. A spec that cannot run comes back **200 with `valid:false`**, not 4xx: the question was "can this run", the server answered it, and the request succeeded.

On top of the pure rules, the endpoint answers the two questions `jobspec` deliberately does not, because the database owns them:

- **Does the content exist?** Every `push`/`install` digest is looked up in `farm.artifacts` in one round trip. Finding out here costs one request; finding out later costs one lease.
- **What does a reset expand to *here*?** Only with a `profile`, because without one the farm does not know which packages the tier owns and guessing would show an operator a plan that is not the plan. This also catches step-id collisions: `ResetSteps` produces ids stable for a tier and package list, so two resets of the same tier expand into identical ids — which `farm.jobs.checkpoint` could not tell apart on a resume.

Response bounds exist for a measured reason: before them, one authenticated request produced a 1.4 GB response body in 21 seconds of CPU, and `writeJSON` marshals into a buffer before writing. A control plane that OOMs cannot answer renewals, and every holder then runs out its TTL and loses its device — #663 reached through the front door. So `problems` is capped at 500, expansions at 16, rendered reset steps at 2000 — with the true counts always reported beside the cap.

**Two things to know before you rely on any of this.** `POST /api/v1/jobs` does not validate at all, and `ctl validate` / `ctl submit` parse *locally* and never call this endpoint — so the CLI cannot tell you a digest is missing or that two resets collide. Only `POST /api/v1/specs/validate` runs the database checks. Both are in Gaps.

sections.heading: Reading a run afterwards
sections.body:
There is no API for step rows. Everything below is SQL against `farm.job_steps` and `farm.job_attempts` (see Gaps).

Step states are `pending`, `running`, `ok`, `failed`, `skipped`, `aborted`. `aborted` means the run context ended mid-step — fencing or shutdown — which is not the step failing; it was stopped. `failed` with `error = 'runner: job max_runtime elapsed'` is the one case where an abort is recorded as a failure, because that clock is the user's own.

`detail` is jsonb and carries, for every step, the payload's own fields (from `stepDetail`) plus `transport_retries`, plus whatever the executor added. `recordStep` merges with `detail || EXCLUDED.detail`, so a re-recorded step accumulates rather than replaces.

Output is bounded at **64 KiB** per step (`DefaultMaxOutput`), applied to the byte slices *before* any string conversion — a single instrumented test can emit hundreds of megabytes, and converting all of it just to keep the first 64 KiB would copy every byte into the heap twice on a host running sixty of these. Truncation appends `… [truncated: N bytes captured, M stored]` and sets `output_truncated`. All device bytes are run through `strings.ToValidUTF8` and stripped of NULs, because Postgres rejects `U+0000` outright and one NUL out of a crashed process would lose the whole row that explains why the job failed.

The job's scratch directory on the device is `/data/local/tmp/device-farmer/<job-uuid>` (`DefaultWorkRoot`, keyed on job id so two jobs sharing a device over time never read each other's files). Staged APKs land at `<work_dir>/<sha256>.apk`. Detached logs and result files go wherever `result_path` says, which need not be under the work directory — which is why the wrapper's `mkdir` is fatal.

rows: How many times the wire failed and was retried inside the lease. Non-zero on an `ok` step is a device to watch, not a job to fix.
Total probes vs. probes that never reached the device. Distinguishes "the condition never became true" from "we could barely reach the device".
The step failed and the spec said carry on.
This attempt found the earlier run's marker files and did not start a second copy.
Whether anything is actually running, and whether `setsid` was available.
False means the transfer was skipped because `farm.device_artifacts` already claimed the content at this path.
The pulled bytes already existed in the store under the same digest.
How many artifact claims were retracted before the wipe, or why they were not.
What the tier actually expanded to on this job. `sub_steps: 0` means it did nothing.
True byte count vs. what was stored.

examples.label: The one query to run when a job failed
examples.code:
SELECT attempt, step_index, step_id, kind, state, exit_code,
       finished_at - started_at AS took,
       (detail->>'transport_retries')::int AS retries,
       left(coalesce(error,''), 120) AS error
  FROM farm.job_steps
 WHERE job_id = '<uuid>'
 ORDER BY attempt, step_index;
examples.note: Real output for job ac52f606-4115-43b3-a58c-c5eee949a0a3. `exit_code` is NULL for kinds that have no single exit status of their own — reset, shell_detached, sleep.

examples.label: Is this a job problem or a device problem?
examples.code:
-- for one job:
SELECT attempt, device_id, fence, outcome, left(coalesce(error,''),100) AS error
  FROM farm.job_attempts WHERE job_id = '<uuid>' ORDER BY attempt;

-- fleet-wide, which devices keep losing attempts:
SELECT device_id,
       count(*) FILTER (WHERE outcome='failed') AS failed,
       count(*) AS attempts
  FROM farm.job_attempts GROUP BY 1
 HAVING count(*) FILTER (WHERE outcome='failed') > 0
 ORDER BY failed DESC;

-- and the fleet-wide outcome census:
SELECT outcome, count(*) FROM farm.job_attempts GROUP BY 1 ORDER BY 2 DESC;
examples.output:
outcome  | count
-----------+-------
 succeeded |  1164
 failed    |    40
 abandoned |     3
           |     1     -- NULL: one row nothing ever closed
examples.note: Snapshot at 10:55. The three `abandoned` rows are leases fenced mid-step — nothing failed. The NULL row was 19 minutes old with its step still `running`; nothing sweeps it (see Gaps). A NULL row seconds old is just an attempt in flight.

sections.heading: Gaps closed since this page was written
sections.body:
The gap list below was written against an earlier tree, and part of it has since been fixed. Those entries are recorded here rather than deleted: a reader who remembers a gap needs to be able to tell **fixed** from **never there**, and the change that closed one is usually the shortest true description of what the behaviour is now.

The rule for this table is the rule for the gap list itself. An entry moves here only after the code was read and the claim checked against it, never because a commit message said so — which is exactly how the list went stale in the first place. Everything still open is in **What is not built here**, immediately below.

rows: `POST /api/v1/jobs` did not validate the spec. `specSubmissionError` was documented as "the gate POST /api/v1/jobs applies to a spec" and was called from nowhere; `handleJobCreate` inserted `req.Spec` straight into `farm.jobs.spec`. Seven jobs reached `failed` with `jobspec: invalid spec`, each having burned a real device.

`internal/api/jobs.go:331` calls `s.ValidateJobSubmission` before the insert. The gate is `internal/api/jobs_submit.go`, and it reaches `specSubmissionError` at line 215; a refusal names every problem at once, with its JSON pointer, rather than failing on the first.

`ctl validate` and `ctl submit` never called the server's validator. Both ran `jobspec.Parse` locally, so `ctl validate` exited 0 on a spec naming digests that are not in the store — the same file came back `valid:false` over HTTP.

Both commands now go through `POST /api/v1/specs/validate` — `internal/ctl/commands_spec.go`, wired at `internal/ctl/ctl.go:701-702`. The local parse still runs first, so a spec with nine defects produces nine messages and no half-created job, and `-o json` renders the API's own schema rather than a second one.
`farm.jobs.profile_id` was written by no code path, so every `reset` step above tier `none` expanded to zero sub-steps, reported `state = ok`, and cleaned nothing.

`JobSubmissionOptions` (`internal/api/jobs_submit.go:75-78`) carries it, `handleJobCreate` writes it (`internal/api/jobs.go:343-346`), and `ctl submit --profile` sets the column instead of a selector key. An unknown profile is refused at submission with the permitted list attached.

`reset_tier`, `max_attempts` and `resumable` — three columns the runner reads on every placement — were not settable through the API or the CLI. Every job on the farm ran with `max_attempts` 3 and `resumable` true whether or not that suited it.

All three are on `JobSubmissionOptions`, validated against the CHECK domains and against `farm.jobs.max_attempts`'s `int32` ceiling (which the constraint cannot catch), and exposed as `ctl submit --reset-tier` and `--max-attempts`. `resumable:false` is a real choice and `max_attempts:0` is a bug worth naming, so both are pointers rather than zero values.

Neither `farm.job_steps` nor `farm.job_attempts` had any route, CLI command or dashboard surface. The two tables built to answer "which step failed" and "is this a job problem or a device problem" were reachable only through psql.

`GET /api/v1/jobs/{id}/steps` and `GET /api/v1/jobs/{id}/attempts` (`internal/api/jobsteps.go`, registered at `cmd/farmd/roles.go:147-154`), scoped with the same rule `GET /api/v1/jobs/{id}` uses and writing nothing; plus `ctl job steps <id>` and `ctl job attempts <id>` (`internal/ctl/commands_job.go`).

Nothing closed an attempt or step row whose process had died. `farm.job_steps` and `farm.job_attempts` had one writer and no sweeper, so a job could read `succeeded` while its step row sat at `running` forever and its attempt row kept `outcome` NULL.

`internal/janitor` sweeps them, and its rule is the LEASE, never the clock: a step is an orphan when its job has no live lease or its own attempt's lease is terminal. A six-hour `shell_detached` step is never swept for looking slow — that would be #663 wearing a different hat. It also re-queues or fails a job whose placement disappeared, and closes stale bulk targets and recovery attempts.
`internal/api` had no test files at all.
`auth_test.go` and `method_test.go`. `internal/runner` and `internal/jobrunner` are still bare — see the gap below.

`jobrunner.Collectors()` (`internal/jobrunner/jobrunner.go:1649`) returns nineteen metrics and is never called. `cmd/farmd/roles.go:86` calls `obs.RegisterAll(reg, log)` with no variadic groups, and the signature is `RegisterAll(r, log, groups ...[]prometheus.Collector)` — so the registry receives internal/obs's own nine collectors and nothing else. Ten packages define `Collectors()` (adbwire, enroll, janitor, jobrunner, node, reaper, recovery, scheduler, topo, watchdog) and the whole tree holds exactly ONE call site: `internal/api/server.go:369`, for adbwire — and that line sits inside `if ownRegistry`, a branch `farmd` never takes, because `runAPI` supplies the registry itself at `roles.go:138`. So in the shipped binary not one package's collectors reach `/metrics`, adbwire's included. `internal/runner` defines no metrics at all — the package does not import prometheus.

Registered with the other nine groups in `newRegistry`, with a test that fails the build if a package's group is dropped. The four terminal states of `farm_jobrunner_outcomes_total` are also touched at registration: a CounterVec with no children exports nothing at all, so the failure-rate alert over it was silently unarmed on any farm where no job had ended yet.

`internal/runner` and `internal/jobrunner` have no test files at all. `go test ./internal/runner/ ./internal/jobrunner/` reports `[no test files]` for both. `internal/api` is covered now (see the table above) and `./internal/jobspec` passes, including `TestKindTableMatchesMigration`, which pins the Go vocabulary to the migration.

3,904 lines across six files. The one that needed a seam is `TestAFencedProcessReleasesNothing`: `releaseLease` refuses to release a lease this process was fenced out of, and that is NOT redundant with the database, because `farm.lease_acquire` re-attaches at the same fence and a fenced process therefore still presents a fence that matches. Only the holder can tell the two placements apart, so `leaseHolder` — Fenced and Release, nothing that can acquire or renew — lets a stub drive it.

A `shell_detached` command's exit code is never checked by the runner. `execShellDetached` (internal/runner/steps.go:340) returns once the launch succeeds; `reattachDetached` (steps.go:411-414) only tests `result_path` for existence; nothing anywhere reads its contents.

The wrapper publishes the status and the probe accepts exactly three shapes: `absent`, `running`, and `done` followed by an exit status. Anything else is an answer we did not understand, and the one reading it must never become is "absent" — which would start a second copy of a command that may well still be running. It is retried inside the lease instead.

sections.source: internal/api/jobs_submit.go, internal/api/jobsteps.go, internal/ctl/commands_spec.go, internal/ctl/commands_job.go, internal/janitor/janitor.go, cmd/farmd/roles.go

gaps.what: push, install and pull have never completed on this deployment, and push actively fails. `farm.job_steps` holds one `push` and two `install` rows, all in state `aborted`, and no `pull` row at all. Every push attempt records a `state = 'failed'` row in `farm.device_artifacts` with `detail.error` = `adbwire: stream_write: peer_closed … wsasend: An established connection was aborted` — three devices so far.
gaps.consequence: I submitted job 42f3c6be-4ee5-4b58-8df2-e16072885708 (push → install → shell → pull) against the one real artifact in the store (harness.apk, a27cf114…3deca). The push retried the wire seven times over 60 seconds inside its lease and never transferred a byte; the step ended `aborted` when the lease was fenced. The execution paths documented above from the code — `EnsureOnDevice`'s ledger skip and its verification, the device-side copy fallback, the streamed pull into the content store, the `pm install` double-check — have not been observed working on any device here. Test them on staging hardware before relying on them. One thing worth knowing: a `failed` row in `farm.device_artifacts` is a record, not a poison pill — `EnsureOnDevice` skips only on `state = 'present'` (internal/artifacts/store.go:875), so the next job re-pushes.

gaps.what: On this demo box a simulated worker (`actor='demo'`, internal/demo/demo.go:1233-1260 and 2033) drives some of the same jobs the real jobrunner is executing, releases their leases, and writes `farm.jobs.state` directly.
gaps.consequence: Job and step rows contradict each other here in ways production would not produce, and the contradiction is not passive — it fences real runs. Watch job 42f3c6be: `job_attempt_started` from actor `runner` at 10:52:20 on device e0d50645 at fence 2389; `job_succeeded` from actor `demo` at 10:52:35 claiming `steps: 4`; the lease released with reason `completed` at 10:52:35 by the demo; and the runner's own push step, still retrying, ending `aborted` with `lease: fenced`. Fleet-wide, `farm.events` shows 92 `job_succeeded` events from `demo` alongside 1183 `job_attempt_finished` from `runner`. When reading this farm, trust the `runner` actor's rows, and treat a job state that no attempt row supports as a demo artefact.

INVARIANT CHECK: I read every section for anything implying a connectivity failure can end a lease. Two places in the draft came close and are now corrected. First, the install/push rows in state 'aborted' were described as ending "after 7 transport retries", which reads as the retries ending them; their actual error is 'lease: fenced' with attempt outcome 'abandoned', and the text now says so and uses them as the counter-example.
